subject: maths
title: Chapter 9 · Test 4
summary: Chapter 9 test 4: 15 questions on sampling, box plots, standard deviation, scatterplots, time series and evaluating statistical reports.
body: This test covers Chapter 9 · Statistics: collecting data and sampling, box plots and the five-number summary, standard deviation, scatterplots and lines of best fit, time-series data and evaluating statistical reports. It has 15 multiple-choice questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes and work with no notes. A calculator is allowed for this test, but show your working on paper so you can check each step. Many questions use a graph or diagram — read the axes and scales carefully before you answer.

questions.prompt: To find out how residents feel about public transport, a council hands out a survey only to people on one train. What is the main problem?

options.A: Non-response bias: nobody answers surveys on trains
options.C: Selection bias: people already on a train may not represent all residents
options.D: Nothing — train passengers know about public transport

questions.explanation: Only train passengers could be chosen, so people who don't use public transport are left out — selection bias. Nothing in the question suggests the wording was leading.
steps: Ask: who could be chosen? Only people on one train.
They are not a representative mix of all residents — selection bias.

mistakes.A: Step 1: we are not told about who answered. The problem is who could be ASKED.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the wording of the question was not given. Look at who received the survey.
mistakes.D: Step 2: they know about trains, but they are not a fair mix of all residents (for example, people who drive).

questions.prompt: Which data set has a standard deviation of 0?
questions.explanation: All values equal the mean (5), so every deviation is 0 and the standard deviation is 0. In −1, 0, 1 the mean is 0, but the values are still spread out.
steps: A standard deviation of 0 means no spread: every value equals the mean.
Only 5, 5, 5, 5 has all values the same.

mistakes.B: Step 1: these values are not all the same, so there is some spread.
mistakes.C: Step 1: these values differ from their mean of 2.5, so the spread is not 0.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the MEAN is 0, but the values still spread out from it.

questions.topic: Scatterplots and lines of best fit
questions.prompt: The scatterplot shows daily screen time and nightly sleep for 11 teenagers. What type of correlation does it show?

options.D: It cannot be described without a line of best fit

questions.explanation: As screen time goes up, sleep goes down — the dots fall from left to right — so the correlation is negative.
steps: Look at the direction: as screen time increases, sleep decreases.
Falling from left to right means negative correlation.

mistakes.A: Step 1: as screen time increases, the dots go DOWN, so it is negative.
mistakes.C: Step 1: there is a clear downward pattern in the dots.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you can describe the direction just by looking at the dots.

questions.diagram_alt: Scatterplot of sleep against screen time for 11 teenagers; the dots fall steadily from about 9.6 hours of sleep at 1 hour of screen time to 6.7 hours at 6 hours

questions.topic: Box plots and the five-number summary
questions.prompt: The box plot shows the number of emails a worker received each day. What is the lower quartile (Q1)?
questions.explanation: Q1 is the left-hand end of the box: 10 emails. 6 is the minimum, at the end of the whisker.
steps: The box runs from Q1 to Q3.
Its left-hand end is at 10, so Q1 = 10.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 6 is the end of the left whisker — the minimum. Q1 is the left end of the box.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 16 is the line inside the box — the median.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 19 is the right end of the box — Q3.

questions.diagram_alt: A box plot of emails per day on a scale from 5 to 30: minimum 6, Q1 10, median 16, Q3 19, maximum 28

questions.prompt: In a random sample of 120 students from a school of 900, 42 said they would join a coding club. Estimate how many students at the school would join.
questions.explanation: 42 ÷ 120 = 0.35, and 0.35 × 900 = 315. Answering 35 stops at the percentage instead of applying it to the school.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 42 is the number in the sample. Scale it up to the 900 students.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 585 is the estimate of students who would NOT join.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 35 is the PERCENTAGE of the sample. Find 35% of 900.

questions.prompt: The graph shows solar panels installed in a town, with a dashed trend line through (2018, 25) and (2023, 40). If the trend continues, forecast the number (in hundreds) for 2026.
questions.explanation: Gradient = (40 − 25) ÷ 5 = 3 hundred per year, so 2026 is 40 + 3 × 3 = 49 hundred. Stopping at 2025 gives 46.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 46 is the forecast for 2025. From 2023 to 2026 is 3 years.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 9 is only the increase from 2023 to 2026. Add it to 40.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the gradient is 15 ÷ 5 = 3 per year, not 5 per year. Divide the rise by the number of years.

questions.diagram_alt: Time-series graph of solar panels installed in hundreds from 2018 to 2023: 26, 27, 32, 33, 37, 40, with a dashed trend line from (2018, 25) to (2023, 40); the time axis runs to 2027

questions.topic: Box plots and the five-number summary
questions.prompt: Find the upper quartile (Q3) of these 11 values: 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 20.
questions.explanation: The median is 11; the upper half 12, 14, 15, 18, 20 has median 15. Including 11 in the upper half gives 14.5 instead.
steps: 11 values: the median is the 6th value, 11.
Leave it out: the upper half is 12, 14, 15, 18, 20.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you included the median (11) in the upper half. With 11 values, leave it out: the upper half is 12, 14, 15, 18, 20.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 18 is the 4th value of the upper half. The middle of 5 values is the 3rd.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 11 is the median of all the data. Q3 is the median of the upper half.

questions.prompt: A headline uses this graph and says "Petrol prices skyrocket!" By what percentage did the price actually rise, correct to 1 decimal place?
questions.explanation: The rise is $1.95 − $1.85 = $0.10, and 0.10 ÷ 1.85 × 100 ≈ 5.4%. The bars only look tripled because the axis starts at $1.80.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 200% comes from the bar heights above $1.80 (April's bar looks 3 times as tall). Use the real prices.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 10 is the rise in CENTS. Divide the 10-cent rise by the March price, $1.85.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you divided by April's $1.95. Divide by the starting price, $1.85.

questions.diagram_alt: Column graph of petrol prices: March $1.85 and April $1.95 per litre, on a vertical axis from $1.80 to $2.00 with a zig-zag break

questions.topic: Scatterplots and lines of best fit
questions.prompt: A line of best fit passes through (0, 8) and (5, 23). Find its equation.
questions.explanation: m = (23 − 8) ÷ (5 − 0) = 3 and the line meets the y-axis at 8, so y = 3x + 8. Swapping the numbers (y = 8x + 3) mixes up gradient and intercept.
steps: The line passes through (0, 8), so c = 8.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the gradient and intercept are swapped. The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 8), so c = 8.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 23 ÷ 5 ignores that the line starts at 8. The rise is 23 − 8 = 15.
mistakes.D: Step 2: c is the y-value when x = 0, which is 8, not 23.

questions.prompt: The dot plot shows the number of text messages 9 friends sent in an hour. Find the population standard deviation, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Mean 5; squared deviations 16, 4, 4, 0, 0, 0, 4, 4, 16 total 48; σ = √(48 ÷ 9) ≈ 2.31. Forgetting the square root gives 5.33.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 48 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.33 is the variance. Take the square root.
mistakes.C: Step 3: √(48 ÷ 8) divides by n − 1. Population σ divides by n = 9.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 16 ÷ 9 averages the plain distances. Square each deviation first.

questions.diagram_alt: Dot plot of text messages sent by 9 friends on a scale from 0 to 10: one dot at 1, two at 3, three at 5, two at 7 and one at 9, with the mean 5 marked

questions.prompt: A gym recorded 45, 52, 49, 56, 60, 58, 64 visitors on seven days. What is the LAST 3-point moving average, correct to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: The last 3-point moving average uses days 5–7: (60 + 58 + 64) ÷ 3 = 182 ÷ 3 ≈ 60.67. Averaging just two values gives 61.
steps: The last three values are 60, 58 and 64.

mistakes.B: Step 1: (58 + 64) ÷ 2 averages only two values. Use the last three: 60, 58, 64.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 182 is the total of the last three values. Divide by 3.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 58 is the middle value of the last three, not their mean.

questions.topic: Box plots and the five-number summary
questions.prompt: The box plot shows the scores of 80 students in a quiz. About how many students scored between 20 and 44?
questions.explanation: From Q1 (20) to the maximum (44) covers three of the four sections, about 75% of 80 = 60 students. 40 counts only the box.
steps: 20 is Q1 and 44 is the maximum.
From Q1 to the maximum is three quarters of the data: 75%.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 40 students is 50% — just the box. From 20 (Q1) to 44 (the maximum) is three quarters.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 20 students is one quarter. From Q1 to the maximum covers three sections.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 44 − 20 = 24 is a distance on the scale, not a number of students.

questions.diagram_alt: A box plot of quiz scores for 80 students on a scale from 10 to 45: minimum 12, Q1 20, median 26, Q3 31, maximum 44

questions.prompt: A study found that students who eat breakfast get higher marks on average. A report concludes: "Eating breakfast causes higher marks." Which is the best evaluation?

options.A: The conclusion is proven, because the correlation is positive
options.B: The data shows an association, but other factors (like sleep or home support) could explain both, so cause is not proven
options.C: The conclusion is wrong, because breakfast and marks are not related
options.D: The conclusion is proven if the sample was large

questions.explanation: A correlation shows the two variables move together, but a lurking variable such as sleep or family routine could affect both. A positive correlation alone does not prove cause.
steps: The study shows an association between breakfast and marks.
Other factors (sleep, routine, home support) could cause both, so the report cannot claim breakfast causes higher marks.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a correlation alone never proves cause. Think of a lurking variable.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the study DID find a relationship. The issue is whether it is cause.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a large sample makes the association more certain, but it still does not prove cause.

questions.topic: Box plots and the five-number summary
questions.prompt: Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to find the outlier(s) in: 2, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 21, 23.
questions.explanation: Q1 = 14.5, Q3 = 20, IQR = 5.5, so the fences are 6.25 and 28.25. Only 2 is outside them. 23 is the largest value but is inside the upper fence.
steps: 8 values: lower half 2, 14, 15, 16 gives Q1 = 14.5; upper half 18, 19, 21, 23 gives Q3 = 20.
Only 2 is beyond a fence, so only 2 is an outlier.

mistakes.A: Step 3: the upper fence is 20 + 8.25 = 28.25, so 23 is inside it.
mistakes.B: Step 3: the lower fence is 14.5 − 8.25 = 6.25, and 2 is below it.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 14 is above the lower fence of 6.25, so it is not an outlier.

questions.topic: Scatterplots and lines of best fit
questions.prompt: For a car, the line of best fit linking trip distance d (km) and fuel used F (litres) is F = 0.07d + 0.5, made from trips of 50 to 400 km. Fuel costs $2 per litre. Predict the fuel cost of a 300 km trip.
questions.explanation: F = 0.07 × 300 + 0.5 = 21.5 L, and 21.5 × $2 = $43; 300 km is inside the data, so the prediction is fair. Leaving out the 0.5 gives $42.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 0.07 × 300 = 21 L forgets the + 0.5. The fuel is 21.5 L.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 21.5 is the fuel in LITRES. Multiply by $2 per litre.
mistakes.D: Steps 1 and 2: 21 forgets the + 0.5 and is still in litres. Find 21.5 L, then multiply by $2.
